hook.text: "All men are mortal" hides ambiguity. Replace words with symbols and the meaning becomes razor-sharp.

buildup.text: Natural language is messy. "I saw the man with the telescope" has two readings. Logic removes that fog.

discovery.text: Formal logic replaces words with symbols so we can check reasoning mechanically, like solving equations.

twist.text: Computers run on formal logic. Every circuit in your phone evaluates symbolic true-or-false statements.

climax.text: Symbols don't make logic harder—they make it unambiguous. Precision is the whole point.

quiz.question: Why does formal logic use symbols?

hook.text: In formal logic, "It is raining" becomes just P. One letter carries the entire statement.

buildup.text: A proposition is any statement that's either true or false. We assign it a variable: P, Q, R, and so on.

discovery.text: Variables let us study argument structure without caring about content. P → Q works for any P and Q.

twist.text: This abstraction is the power move: one formula proves validity for millions of different real-world arguments.

climax.text: By stripping content away, formal logic reveals that structure alone determines validity.

quiz.question: What does a propositional variable like P represent?
options: A statement that is true or false

hook.text: Five tiny symbols—and, or, not, if-then, if-and-only-if—can express any logical thought.

buildup.text: AND (∧) is true when both parts are true. OR (∨) is true when at least one is. NOT (¬) flips the truth.

discovery.text: IF-THEN (→) says: if the first is true, the second must be. Only false when P is true but Q is false.

twist.text: IFF (↔) requires both sides to match: both true or both false. It's the strictest connective.

climax.text: Every complex argument, no matter how tangled, can be built from combinations of these five connectives.

quiz.question: When is an OR (∨) statement true?
options: Only when both parts are true
When at least one part is true

hook.text: Negating "All cats are black" isn't "No cats are black." Getting negation wrong is a classic mistake.

buildup.text: NOT (¬) simply flips truth to false and false to true. ¬P is the opposite of P.

discovery.text: The negation of "all" is "at least one is not." Not "none." This trips up even experienced thinkers.

twist.text: Double negation—¬¬P—brings you back to P. Two flips restore the original truth value.

climax.text: Mastering negation prevents the most common errors in formal reasoning and everyday arguments.

punchline.text: Flip once carefully. Flip twice, you're back.

quiz.question: What is the negation of 'All birds can fly'?
options: At least one bird cannot fly

hook.text: Not every string of symbols is meaningful. "P → ∧ Q" is nonsense—formal logic has grammar rules.

buildup.text: A well-formed formula (WFF) follows strict syntax: correct connectives between proper propositions.

discovery.text: "(P ∧ Q) → R" is well-formed. "P ∧ → Q" is not. Parentheses and order matter.

twist.text: Just like natural language needs grammar, formal logic needs syntax to prevent ambiguity and errors.

climax.text: Only WFFs can be evaluated for truth. Ill-formed strings have no truth value—they're just noise.

quiz.question: What is a well-formed formula?
options: A logically correct sentence following syntax rules

hook.text: How do you prove a logical formula works for every possible input? List them all in a table.

buildup.text: A truth table lists every combination of true/false for each variable, then evaluates the whole formula.

discovery.text: Two variables make four rows. Three make eight. Each new variable doubles the rows: 2^n combinations.

twist.text: Truth tables are brute-force but foolproof. If the formula holds in every row, it's a tautology.

climax.text: They're the simplest proof method in logic—no creativity needed, just careful bookkeeping.

quiz.question: How many rows does a truth table with 3 variables have?

hook.text: "I'll come if it's sunny AND I'm free." Both conditions needed. Change AND to OR and the rules shift.

buildup.text: P ∧ Q is true only when both P and Q are true. One false input makes the whole thing false.

discovery.text: P ∨ Q is true when at least one is true. It's only false when both P and Q are false.

twist.text: English "or" is often exclusive (one or the other). Logical OR is inclusive—both can be true.

climax.text: Mixing up AND and OR in conditions causes bugs in code, contracts, and legal documents constantly.

punchline.text: AND demands both. OR needs just one.

quiz.question: When is P ∧ Q (P AND Q) true?

hook.text: "If pigs fly, I'll give you a million dollars." Pigs don't fly. Is my promise broken? Formally: no.

buildup.text: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. In all other cases, the conditional is true.

discovery.text: When P is false, P → Q is true regardless of Q. This is called a "vacuously true" conditional.

twist.text: This shocks beginners. "If 2+2=5 then I'm the Pope" is technically true in formal logic.

climax.text: The material conditional doesn't match everyday "if-then" perfectly, but it makes formal systems consistent.

quiz.question: When is P → Q false?
options: When P is true and Q is false

hook.text: "It's either raining or not raining." True no matter what. That's a tautology—always true by structure.

buildup.text: A tautology is a formula that's true in every row of its truth table. P ∨ ¬P is the classic example.

discovery.text: A contradiction is always false. P ∧ ¬P—something is both true and false—fails in every row.

twist.text: Contingent formulas are neither: sometimes true, sometimes false depending on the variable values.

climax.text: Tautologies are logical laws. They hold regardless of facts—pure structural guarantees.

quiz.question: What is a tautology?

hook.text: Is this argument valid? Build a truth table and the answer jumps out—no guesswork required.

buildup.text: An argument is valid if every row where all premises are true also makes the conclusion true.

discovery.text: Find the rows where premises are true. If even one has a false conclusion, the argument is invalid.

twist.text: A valid argument can have false premises. Validity only guarantees: true inputs → true output.

climax.text: Truth tables give a mechanical, objective test. No intuition needed—just follow the rows.

quiz.question: How do truth tables test validity?
options: Check if the conclusion is always true
Check that true premises always yield a true conclusion

hook.text: "Not (A and B)" equals "not A or not B." Augustus De Morgan found the swap rule that simplifies everything.

buildup.text: De Morgan's first law: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ (¬P ∨ ¬Q). Negate AND, distribute, flip to OR.

discovery.text: Second law: ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ (¬P ∧ ¬Q). Negate OR, distribute, flip to AND. Mirror image of the first.

twist.text: Programmers use De Morgan constantly. Simplifying complex conditions makes code easier to read and debug.

climax.text: These two laws let you rewrite any negated compound statement into a simpler equivalent form.

punchline.text: Negate and flip: AND becomes OR.

quiz.question: What does ¬(P ∧ Q) equal according to De Morgan's laws?

hook.text: "If it rains, the ground is wet" means exactly the same as "If the ground is dry, it didn't rain."

buildup.text: The contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P. Flip both parts and negate them. Always equivalent.

discovery.text: The converse (Q → P) is NOT equivalent. "If the ground is wet, it rained" could be wrong—sprinklers.

twist.text: The inverse (¬P → ¬Q) also fails equivalence. Only the contrapositive preserves truth perfectly.

climax.text: Contrapositive reasoning is a proof technique: prove the contrapositive to prove the original.

quiz.question: What is the contrapositive of 'If P then Q'?
options: If not Q then not P
If not P then not Q

hook.text: In math, a(b + c) = ab + ac. Logic has the same trick: AND distributes over OR, and vice versa.

buildup.text: P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R). AND distributes over OR just like multiplication over addition.

discovery.text: P ∨ (Q ∧ R) ≡ (P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ R). OR distributes over AND too—a symmetry math doesn't have.

twist.text: In algebra, addition doesn't distribute over multiplication. Logic is more symmetric than arithmetic.

climax.text: Distribution lets you expand or factor logical formulas—essential for simplification and proofs.

punchline.text: Expand or factor—logic goes both ways.

quiz.question: What does P ∧ (Q ∨ R) equal?

hook.text: "You pass if and only if you score above 70." Both directions must hold—not just one.

buildup.text: P ↔ Q means P → Q AND Q → P. Both the conditional and its converse must be true.

discovery.text: P ↔ Q is true when P and Q match (both true or both false). It's false when they disagree.

twist.text: "If and only if" is much stronger than just "if." Dropping "only if" halves the requirement.

climax.text: Definitions in math use biconditionals. "Even" means n = 2k if and only if n is divisible by 2.

quiz.question: When is P ↔ Q true?
options: When P and Q have the same truth value

hook.text: Two formulas look different but mean the same thing. How do you prove they're logically equivalent?

buildup.text: Method one: build truth tables for both and check that every row matches. Brute force but reliable.

discovery.text: Method two: use known equivalence laws—De Morgan, distribution, double negation—to transform one into the other.

twist.text: Method two is faster but requires creativity. Method one always works but grows exponentially with variables.

climax.text: Logical equivalence is the backbone of simplification—in proofs, circuits, and programming.

quiz.question: What proves two formulas logically equivalent?

hook.text: "All dogs are loyal" can't be expressed with P and Q alone. You need a more powerful language.

buildup.text: Propositional logic treats whole statements as atoms. Predicate logic looks inside—at subjects and properties.

discovery.text: "D(x)" means "x is a dog." "L(x)" means "x is loyal." Now you can write: for all x, D(x) → L(x).

twist.text: This jump from propositional to predicate logic was one of the biggest leaps in the history of reasoning.

climax.text: Predicate logic can express relationships, quantities, and structures that propositional logic simply cannot.

quiz.question: What does predicate logic add beyond propositional logic?

hook.text: "Every student passed." In symbols: ∀x (S(x) → P(x)). The upside-down A means "for all."

buildup.text: The universal quantifier (∀) asserts that a property holds for every member of a domain.

discovery.text: ∀x P(x) is true only if P(x) is true for every single x. One exception makes it false.

twist.text: The domain matters enormously. "All numbers are positive" is false for integers but true for natural numbers.

climax.text: Universal statements are bold claims. They're easy to disprove—just find one counterexample.

quiz.question: What does the symbol ∀ mean?

hook.text: "Some birds can't fly." One example is enough: penguins. In symbols: ∃x (B(x) ∧ ¬F(x)).

buildup.text: The existential quantifier (∃) asserts that at least one member of the domain satisfies the property.

discovery.text: ∃x P(x) is true if there's even one x making P(x) true. Just one is enough.

twist.text: "There exists" is humble. It doesn't say how many—just that the count isn't zero.

climax.text: Existential claims are proven by example. Finding one witness makes the whole statement true.

quiz.question: How do you prove an existential statement?

hook.text: Negating "everyone is happy" doesn't give "nobody is happy." It gives "someone isn't happy."

buildup.text: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Negating "for all" flips to "there exists one that doesn't."

discovery.text: ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Negating "there exists" flips to "none do."

twist.text: These are the De Morgan's laws for quantifiers. Same pattern: negate, flip the quantifier, negate inside.

climax.text: Getting quantifier negation right prevents the most common logical errors in philosophy and law.

quiz.question: What is ¬∀x P(x) equivalent to?

hook.text: "Everyone loves someone" and "someone is loved by everyone" use the same words—but mean different things.

buildup.text: ∀x ∃y L(x,y): for every person, there's someone they love. Each person can love a different someone.

discovery.text: ∃y ∀x L(x,y): there's one person everyone loves. A single beloved individual.

twist.text: Order matters! Swapping ∀ and ∃ changes meaning completely. This catches even experienced logicians.

climax.text: Read nested quantifiers from left to right. The outer one sets the scope for the inner one.

punchline.text: Same words, swap order, new meaning.

quiz.question: Does swapping ∀ and ∃ change the meaning?
options: Yes, it can completely change the meaning

hook.text: A proof isn't persuasion. It's a chain of steps where each follows unavoidably from the last.

buildup.text: In formal logic, a proof starts from axioms or premises and applies inference rules to reach a conclusion.

discovery.text: Every step must be justified by a specific rule: modus ponens, generalization, substitution, and so on.

twist.text: A proof that skips a step is no proof at all. Rigor is what separates demonstration from hand-waving.

climax.text: Proofs make truth mechanical. A computer can check every step without understanding the subject.

quiz.question: What must every step in a formal proof have?
options: A justification by an inference rule

hook.text: The most straightforward strategy: start with what you know and march step by step to the conclusion.

buildup.text: A direct proof assumes the premises are true, applies rules, and derives the conclusion. No tricks.

discovery.text: Prove: if n is even, then n² is even. Let n = 2k. Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is even. Done.

twist.text: Direct proofs are clean but not always possible. Some conclusions resist a forward march.

climax.text: When a direct path exists, take it. It's the most transparent and convincing proof method.

quiz.question: How does a direct proof work?
options: It assumes the conclusion is false
It derives the conclusion from the premises step by step

hook.text: Assume the opposite of what you want to prove. If that leads to nonsense, your original claim must be true.

buildup.text: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) assumes ¬C, then derives a contradiction, proving C.

discovery.text: Prove √2 is irrational: assume it's rational (a/b in lowest terms), and you get both a and b are even. Contradiction.

twist.text: This method is controversial in some math philosophies. Constructivists want to build truth, not just deny falsehood.

climax.text: Contradiction proofs are powerful when direct paths are blocked. They attack from the reverse direction.

punchline.text: Assume the opposite. Watch it break.

quiz.question: What does proof by contradiction assume?

hook.text: Knock down the first domino and prove each one knocks the next. All of them fall.

buildup.text: Mathematical induction proves a statement for all natural numbers in two steps: base case and inductive step.

discovery.text: Base case: show it's true for n=1. Inductive step: assume true for n=k, then prove it for n=k+1.

twist.text: Induction doesn't try every number—that's impossible. It proves the infinite chain holds with just two steps.

climax.text: It's the primary tool for proving things about infinite sequences, sums, and recursive structures.

quiz.question: What are the two steps of mathematical induction?

hook.text: Can't prove it all at once? Split into cases and prove each one separately.

buildup.text: Proof by cases divides the possibilities into exhaustive groups and proves the claim for each group.

discovery.text: Prove |x| ≥ 0: Case 1, x ≥ 0, so |x| = x ≥ 0. Case 2, x < 0, so |x| = -x > 0. Both covered.

twist.text: The cases must be exhaustive—missing one leaves a gap. And they must cover everything, no overlap required.

climax.text: Case analysis is simple but effective. Complex problems often yield to careful splitting.

quiz.question: What requirement must cases satisfy in a proof by cases?

hook.text: Chess has pieces, a board, and rules. A formal system has symbols, axioms, and inference rules.

buildup.text: A formal system defines a language (symbols), starting truths (axioms), and rules for deriving new truths.

discovery.text: Euclidean geometry is one: five axioms, clear rules, and every theorem ever proven follows from them.

twist.text: Change one axiom (like the parallel postulate) and you get a completely different geometry.

climax.text: Formal systems are truth machines—but they're only as good as their axioms and rules.

punchline.text: Axioms define the universe of truths.

quiz.question: What are the components of a formal system?

hook.text: A logical system can have a fatal flaw: proving things that aren't true, or failing to prove things that are.

buildup.text: Soundness means every provable statement is actually true. The system never lies.

discovery.text: Completeness means every true statement is provable. The system misses nothing.

twist.text: Gödel proved that powerful enough systems can't be both complete and consistent. Something must give.

climax.text: We choose soundness: better to miss some truths than to prove falsehoods.

quiz.question: What does soundness guarantee about a logical system?

hook.text: Can a computer always determine whether a logical statement is true or false? Sometimes, no.

buildup.text: A system is decidable if there's an algorithm that can determine the truth of any statement in it.

discovery.text: Propositional logic is decidable—truth tables always work. Predicate logic is not always decidable.

twist.text: Alonzo Church and Alan Turing independently proved this in 1936. Some questions are algorithmically unsolvable.

climax.text: Undecidability isn't a bug—it's a fundamental limit of computation and formal reasoning.

quiz.question: What does it mean for a system to be decidable?
options: An algorithm can determine truth of any statement

hook.text: What if true and false aren't the only options? Several logics throw out the binary.

buildup.text: Three-valued logic adds "unknown." Fuzzy logic allows partial truth. Intuitionistic logic rejects excluded middle.

discovery.text: Fuzzy logic powers washing machines and cruise control—situations where "somewhat true" is more useful than binary.

twist.text: Quantum logic challenges even basic rules: in quantum mechanics, distribution laws can fail.

climax.text: Classical logic isn't wrong—it's just one system. Different domains need different logical tools.

quiz.question: What does fuzzy logic allow?

hook.text: AI, circuits, law, philosophy—formal logic powers systems you use every day without realizing.

buildup.text: Every database query is logic. Every circuit gate is AND, OR, NOT. Every legal contract is an if-then chain.

discovery.text: Formal verification uses logic to prove software has zero bugs—before it even runs.

twist.text: Despite its limits (Gödel, undecidability), formal logic remains the most reliable reasoning tool we have.

climax.text: Where precision matters and ambiguity kills, formal logic is the language humans and machines share.

quiz.question: Where is formal logic used in technology?
